{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-sc-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"d93b84b5dd3de527eb7a96da793a09b0c0ec637af145a990b93cc03f741abbec","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-sc-class-d:lineage:50","source_registry_sha256":"61c32f86a25e3c021742b3c9ddf64a97709817dd75a19df6d2b69eac0a40c4f1","source_liveness_sha256":"feb7871590284d2a19ab0509ff65b48154ba15e637a6ec9b839f55a72736ffdb"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Emergency situations: collision avoidance, ABS, skids, drop-offs, vehicle malfunctions, breakdowns and emergency contact records","heading":"C — Braking with ABS, swerving and accelerating to avoid collisions, skids and pavement drop-offs, brake failure, tire blowouts, power failure, stuck accelerators, breakdowns and SCDMV emergency contact information","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Braking with ABS, swerving and accelerating to avoid collisions, skids and pavement drop-offs, brake failure, tire blowouts, power failure, stuck accelerators, breakdowns and SCDMV emergency contact information
Knowledge domain: what a South Carolina driver does when trouble strikes, from the three ways to avoid a collision and correct ABS braking, through skids and road-edge drop-offs, to handling brake failure, blowouts, engine failure, a stuck accelerator and a breakdown, and recording emergency contacts with SCDMV.

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
Every driver has the responsibility to do everything possible to prevent collisions. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A01
You have three options for avoiding a collision or reducing its impact: braking, steering or accelerating. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A01
Most new vehicles have an anti-lock braking system, or ABS, which lets you stop without skidding while keeping steering control, so read your owner's manual on how to use it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A01
With ABS, press the brake pedal as hard as you can and hold constant pressure, and do not pump the brakes, because pumping deactivates ABS. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A01
ABS works only while you keep pressure on the pedal, and a vibrating pedal or a clicking sound during ABS braking is normal. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A02
You can still steer your vehicle while ABS is active. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A02
Quickly steering around a problem, sometimes called swerving, may let you avoid a collision. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A02
To swerve, hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands and steer the way you want to go while trying to avoid other traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A02
Once past the problem, steer the opposite way to straighten the vehicle, regain control and settle at a suitable speed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A02
Accelerating may be the way to avoid a collision, for example when another vehicle is about to hit you from behind or from the side. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A02
Skids happen when you drive too fast for road conditions, stop suddenly or the tires can no longer grip the road, and once skidding you have little control. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A02
If your vehicle starts to skid, ease off the brake or accelerator, look where you want to go and steer in that direction. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A03
Avoid panic steering, which is trying to get back onto the pavement the instant the wheels leave it at an uneven drop-off. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A03
If an uneven drop-off takes your vehicle off the paved surface, slow down gradually when it is safe and steer gently back onto the pavement. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A03
Going off and coming back onto the road gradually, with only slight steering, reduces the chance of erratic vehicle behavior on an uneven or unpaved shoulder. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A03
Check all warning lights, including the brake light, because a brake warning light means the brakes are not working properly and you should not drive. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A03
If the brakes fail while you drive, use the parking brake, pulling its handle or pushing its pedal slowly so the rear wheels do not lock, and be ready to release it if a skid starts. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A04
If the parking brake does not work either, turn off the engine, find a safe place to slow to a stop off the roadway, and do not keep driving without working brakes. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A04
A tire blowout is a rapid loss of air from a tire, and if a front tire blows out the vehicle pulls sharply toward the side of the blowout. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A04
If a rear tire blows out, the vehicle wobbles, shakes and pulls somewhat toward the side of the blowout. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A04
In a blowout or sudden flat, grip the wheel firmly, keep the vehicle going straight and slow down gradually by taking your foot off the accelerator. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A04
Do not brake after a blowout; let the vehicle slow on its own, or brake gently if you must. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A04
Avoid stopping on the road after a blowout if at all possible; pull off in a safe place, turn on the emergency flashers and have the tire changed and replaced. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A04
If the engine shuts off while driving, keep a strong grip, knowing the steering wheel may be hard to turn but can still be turned. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A04
After an engine failure, look for an escape path and, instead of braking hard, use steady brake pressure to slow down and pull off the roadway. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A05
Once stopped after an engine failure, try to restart it, and if that fails, raise the hood, turn on the emergency flashers and call for help. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A05
If your vehicle is accelerating out of control, the manual says to turn off the engine, shift to neutral and search for an escape path. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A05
With a stuck accelerator, steer smoothly, brake gently, pull off the roadway and have the pedal repaired at a service center before driving again. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A05
If your vehicle breaks down on the highway, make sure others can see it, since collisions often happen when a driver notices a disabled vehicle too late to stop. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A05
If you must stop with vehicle trouble, get off the road and away from traffic if possible and turn on your emergency flashers. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A05
If you carry emergency flares, set them about 200 to 300 feet behind the vehicle so other drivers have time to change lanes. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A06
Holders of a beginner's permit, driver's license or identification card can enter emergency contact information on their SCDMV record through the dmv.sc.gov website. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A06
After a collision or medical emergency, South Carolina law enforcement officers can then see that emergency contact information and may share it with medical personnel. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0108]

Misconceptions: pumping the brakes switches ABS off, so you hold firm, steady pressure; a vibrating ABS pedal is normal and not a fault; after a blowout you do not brake hard but let the vehicle slow; jerking back onto the pavement at a drop-off is the dangerous move; a dead engine does not lock the steering, it only makes it heavier.
Mnemonics: brake, steer or accelerate are the three escape options; for ABS, stomp and stay; for a blowout, grip, glide, pull off; for a breakdown, off the road, flashers on, flares well behind.
Glossary: ABS means anti-lock braking system; swerving means quickly steering around a problem; skid means losing tire grip so the vehicle slides; drop-off means an uneven edge where the pavement meets the shoulder; panic steering means jerking the wheel to get back on the pavement at once; blowout means a rapid loss of air from a tire; escape path means a safe route out of traffic; emergency flashers means the hazard lights that show your vehicle is disabled.
